analysis.one_liner: Requires drug makers to give the patent office the same data they give the FDA, and voids patents withheld.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to stop drug companies from making inconsistent statements to the FDA and the patent office was introduced in September 2023, referred to the health committee, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Drug companies sometimes describe the same drug differently to two government agencies: to the Food and Drug Administration they may downplay a drug's novelty to win approval, while telling the patent office it is highly novel to win broad patents that keep cheaper generic copies off the market. This bill would require drug companies to submit to the patent office everything material they give the FDA about a drug's patents, certify the two sets of information match, and would let generic and biosimilar makers use a company's failure to disclose as a defense if the company sues them for patent infringement. It was introduced by a Democrat and a Republican together, but the Senate health committee never acted on it, and it died when the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who buy prescription drugs, because easier generic and biosimilar competition historically pushes prices down. Generic and biosimilar manufacturers also gain a new defense against patent lawsuits built on patents a brand company obtained without giving the patent office the full picture.

how_it_helps.text: Requires any company seeking or holding FDA drug approval to send the patent office all information material to patentability that it submits to the FDA, and to certify to both agencies that the information is complete and consistent. [S2]

Covers both small-molecule drugs under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and biologics under the Public Health Service Act, including patents on formulations, methods of use, and manufacturing. [S2]

Adds a new defense to patent infringement suits: if a patent owner negligently or intentionally failed to make the required disclosures, the accused infringer — typically a generic or biosimilar maker — can raise that failure as a defense. [S2]
Makes FDA approval conditional on compliance: an application can be refused if the sponsor failed to certify its disclosures, and failure to comply becomes a prohibited act the FDA can enforce. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug companies, which would face new disclosure duties, the risk that inconsistently obtained patents become unenforceable, and possible approval delays for failing to certify compliance. Some compliance costs could ultimately show up in prices, but the bill's aim is to shorten patent-protected monopolies that cost consumers far more.

drawbacks.text: Adds certification and cross-agency disclosure requirements for every drug application, which creates administrative burden for drug makers and could slow filings if companies are cautious about the compliance condition on FDA approval. [S2]

The non-disclosure defense invites more patent litigation between brand and generic companies, since accused infringers have a new weapon and courts will have to sort out what counts as negligent non-disclosure. [S2]

The bill only reaches patents connected to information submitted to the FDA; much of the patent thicket around a drug consists of later-filed patents on formulations and manufacturing methods that may never touch an FDA submission, so the actual effect on drug prices could be narrower than the title suggests. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside for consumers runs through competition: if brand companies can no longer win or defend broad patents by describing their inventions inconsistently to two agencies, generic and biosimilar copies reach the market sooner and prices fall. The costs are real but modest — added paperwork, more litigation, and possible approval friction — and the main honest objection is design: the bill only covers information connected to FDA submissions, so it nibbles at the patent-thicket problem rather than solving it.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred the bill to its health committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Maggie Hassan introduced the bill on September 13, 2023, joined by Republican Senator Mike Braun. [S1] [S2] [S3]
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions. [S4]
The action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, and no roll call — the bill's only action was the referral. [S4]
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill expired with the committee never having acted. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug companies are better off: their patents remain fully enforceable no matter what they told the FDA versus the patent office, and the pressure for cheaper generic and biosimilar competition never got a hearing. No consumer group gained anything from the bill's death.

for.name: Sen. Maggie Hassan
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Hampshire, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require drug makers to give the FDA and the patent office consistent information. [S1] [S2]

for.name: Sen. Mike Braun
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it bipartisan from introduction. [S2] [S3]

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on September 13, 2023 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill's entire action history is the referral. [S4]

against.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never brought the bill to a markup or vote during the two-year Congress. [S4]

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan at introduction — a Democrat and a Republican introduced it together — but only two senators supported it, and no votes were ever taken, so there is no record of a partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would require them to mirror to the patent office everything they tell the FDA and would let generic rivals escape infringement suits based on patents obtained through non-disclosure. It strikes at a practice — describing the same drug inconsistently to two agencies — that keeps monopoly prices in place, so its interest ran against the consumers the bill targeted. [S2]

The new non-disclosure defense gives them a way to defeat patents sued on by brand companies that withheld information from the patent office, letting their cheaper copies reach the market. Their gain is consumers' gain. [S2]

industries.industry: Pharmaceutical patent counsel and law firms
industries.note: New certification duties and a new litigation defense mean more compliance work and more patent litigation for firms that serve the drug industry. [S2]
